**Time: about 20 minutes.**

By the end you will have a GitHub repository, connected to an RStudio project on
your machine, with a live web page attached to it.

Keep this repository. You will add to it in part 2.

::: {.callout-note}
## Screenshots

The RStudio screenshots here are accurate. GitHub redesigns its website
regularly, so the GitHub steps are written as instructions rather than pictures —
if a button has moved, the wording should still get you there.
:::

---

## Step 0 — Before you start (5 min, together)

You should already have git installed, an account on GitHub, and RStudio able to
see git. Check the last one now:

**Tools → Global Options → Git/SVN.** The box *Enable version control interface
for RStudio projects* should be ticked and the *Git executable* path filled in.
If it is empty, git is not installed or RStudio cannot find it — say so now
rather than in ten minutes.

Then, in the R console:

```r
install.packages(c("usethis", "gitcreds"))

usethis::use_git_config(
  user.name  = "Your Name",
  user.email = "you@example.com"
)
```

The email does not have to be the one you use on GitHub, but it is simpler if it
is.

### Store a GitHub token

Git needs a credential to push to GitHub. A personal access token is the
quickest route.

```r
usethis::create_github_token()
```

That opens GitHub in your browser with the right options pre-selected. Give the
token a name, create it, and **copy it** — you will not see it again. Then:

```r
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()
```

and paste the token when prompted.

::: {.callout-tip}
## If something goes wrong here

`usethis::git_sitrep()` prints a report of your git and GitHub configuration and
is usually enough to see what is missing.
:::

---

## Step 1 — Make the repository on GitHub (3 min)

Make it on GitHub **first**, then bring it down. Doing it the other way round
means connecting an existing folder to a remote by hand, which is exactly the
kind of thing we do not have time for.

1. On GitHub, click **New repository** (the **+** at the top right, or the green
   button on your profile's Repositories tab).
2. Name it `blind-analysis-yourname`.
3. Leave it **Public**.
4. Tick **Add a README file**. This matters: it gives the repository a first
   commit, so cloning it is clean, and it gives you a file to edit in a moment.
5. **Create repository**.

---

## Step 2 — Open it in RStudio (3 min)

1. On the repository page, click the green **Code** button and copy the
   **HTTPS** URL. It looks like
   `https://github.com/yourname/blind-analysis-yourname.git`.

   Not the SSH one (`git@github.com:…`) — that needs a key you have not set up.

2. In RStudio: **File → New Project → Version Control → Git**.

3. Paste the URL. The project directory name fills itself in. Choose where to
   put it — somewhere you will find again.

4. **Create Project.**

RStudio reopens in your new project, and there is now a **Git** tab in the top
right pane. That tab is the whole interface for today.

---

## Step 3 — Make a change and send it back (5 min)

1. Open `README.md` in RStudio.

2. Write a couple of lines about yourself — who you are, what you work on.
   Markdown works here, and you will meet it properly in part 2:

   ```md
   # Blind analysis workshop

   Notes and exercises from the analysis blinding workshop.

   - Name
   - Institution
   ```

3. Save.

4. In the **Git** tab, `README.md` now has a yellow `?` or a blue `M` beside it.
   Tick the **Staged** box next to it.

5. Click **Commit**. Write a message saying what you did — "Add name to README"
   is a good message, "update" is not. Commit.

6. Click **Push**.

7. Reload the repository page on GitHub. Your text is there.

::: {.callout-note}
## What just happened

Three separate things: saving (your disk), committing (a named version in git's
history) and pushing (sending it to GitHub). Keeping them separate is the point.
It lets you make five small commits and push them together, and it lets you
write down *why* a change happened, not just that it did.
:::

---

## Step 4 — Make a change on GitHub and pull it back (2 min)

Changes travel both ways, and this is what you will be doing constantly in part
3.

1. On GitHub, click `README.md`, then the pencil icon to edit it.
2. Add a line. **Commit changes** directly to `main`.
3. Back in RStudio, click **Pull** in the Git tab.
4. Your local file now has the line you added in the browser.

If you had also edited the same line locally without pulling first, you would
get a **merge conflict** — git refusing to guess which version wins. Do not go
looking for one now, but that is what the word means when you meet it.

---

## Step 5 — Turn on GitHub Pages (2 min)

This takes two minutes today and saves ten in part 2.

1. In RStudio, create a folder called `docs` in your project, and in it a file
   called `index.md` containing one line:

   ```md
   # Coming soon
   ```

2. Stage both, commit, push.

3. On GitHub: **Settings → Pages**. Under **Build and deployment**, set
   **Source** to *Deploy from a branch*, then choose branch **main** and folder
   **/docs**. Save.

4. Wait a minute, then open
   `https://yourname.github.io/blind-analysis-yourname/`.

You should see *Coming soon*. That is now a public web page that you update by
pushing to git.

::: {.callout-important}
## Keep this repository open

In part 2 you will write a report and render it into that same `docs/` folder.
When you push, this page becomes your report — no settings to change.
:::

---

## If you finish early

- Click **History** in the Git tab and look at what a commit record contains.
- Click **Diff** on a changed file to see the line-by-line view. This is why
  version control wants plain text and is not much use on a `.docx`.
- Click **More → Shell** and type `git log --oneline`. Everything the buttons do
  is a command underneath.
